# Introduction to the Business Problem

Ttareungyi, called Seoul Bike in English, is the public bike-share
system of Seoul. A rider takes a bike at one rental station and returns
it at any station in the city. The city wants bikes to be available in
the hours when people ride. For that it needs a prediction for each
hour: will the hour be High, meaning at least 500 bikes rented in that
hour? The people who plan the bikes have to be able to follow that
prediction.

The dataset has one observation per hour from 1 December 2017 to
30 November 2018, 8,760 hours. The system was closed in some hours, and
we keep only the open hours. For each hour we know the hour of the day,
the weather in that hour (temperature, humidity, wind speed,
visibility, solar radiation, rainfall and snowfall), the season, and
whether the day was a holiday. The outcome is `High`. The number of
bikes rented, `count`, is the outcome in one short section on
predicting the count. It is never used to predict `High`.

The question for this lab: a pruned tree gives
rules that a planner can read. Bagging, a random forest and boosting
combine hundreds of trees, and nobody can read those as rules. How much
better are the combined models on hours they have not seen, and is that
worth giving up the readable rules?

You estimate every model in this notebook. Nothing is loaded from a
saved file. Keep the case PDF and the codebook open while you run code.

**Before you run anything.** Suppose two models make about the same
number of mistakes on hours they have not seen. One is a tree that a
planner can read as a list of rules. The other averages 500 trees and
gives only a probability for each hour. Which one would you give the
planners, and what would you want to see before you decide? Talk this
through with the person next to you. We come back to it in section 7.

# Roadmap

1. **Prepare the bike data and keep comparison hours separate.** Keep
   the open hours, define High, and split the hours into analysis,
   validation and test hours.
2. **Grow, read and prune a tree.** A large tree on the analysis hours,
   the complexity table, and two pruned trees. Follow two 8 am hours
   down the tree.
3. **Compare bagging with a random forest.** 500 trees each. Bagging
   lets every split use all ten predictors; the forest lets each split
   use three. Out-of-bag error.
4. **Read variable importance.** Which predictors the forest relies on.
5. **Estimate boosting and compare learning rates.** Cross-validated
   log-loss for two learning rates, then one boosted model.
6. **Predict the rental count.** A tree, a forest and boosting for the
   number of bikes rented, against a simple average.
7. **Compare class models and commit.** Five models for High on the
   same validation hours. You choose one and write down why.
8. **Report the chosen model on test hours.** Once, for the model you
   chose.
9. **After class: extra questions.** More values of mtry, learning rate
   and depth, the count models, other splits, and importance.

# 1. Prepare the bike data and keep comparison hours separate

```{r}
#| label: setup
# rsample: initial_split() makes the stratified splits.
# rpart: classification and regression trees. rpart.plot: tree plots.
# ranger: bagging and random forests.
# xgboost: boosting. This lab needs xgboost version 3 or later.
# yardstick: roc_auc_vec() computes the area under the ROC curve.
# This chunk stops if a package is missing. It does not install anything.
needed <- c("rsample", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "ranger", "xgboost", "yardstick")
missing <- needed[!vapply(needed, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Install the missing packages in the Console, then render again:\n",
    "install.packages(c(",
    paste0('"', missing, '"', collapse = ", "), "))"
  )
}
if (packageVersion("xgboost") < "3.0.0") {
  stop("This lab needs xgboost version 3 or later. You have version ",
       packageVersion("xgboost"), ".\n",
       'Update it in the Console: install.packages("xgboost")')
}

library(rsample)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(ranger)
library(xgboost)
library(yardstick)

options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
# The file is in latin1 encoding because of the degree sign in two
# variable names.
raw <- read.csv("data/SeoulBikeData.csv", fileEncoding = "latin1",
                check.names = FALSE)
names(raw)

# Why? The original names have spaces, brackets and symbols. This line
# turns each run of those characters into one underscore, so that
# "Temperature(°C)" becomes Temperature_C.
names(raw) <- gsub("^_|_$", "", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", names(raw)))
names(raw)
dim(raw)
sum(is.na(raw))

# Functioning_Day is No when the system was closed.
table(raw$Functioning_Day)
tapply(raw$Rented_Bike_Count, raw$Functioning_Day, max)

# Question: How many hours was the system closed? What was the largest
# number of rentals in a closed hour? Why do we drop those hours
# instead of predicting them?
```

```{r}
#| label: define-high
bikes <- subset(raw, Functioning_Day == "Yes")

# The outcome. Low is the first level and High the second, so every
# probability in this lab is a probability of High.
bikes$High <- factor(ifelse(bikes$Rented_Bike_Count >= 500, "High", "Low"),
                     levels = c("Low", "High"))
bikes$Seasons <- factor(bikes$Seasons,
                        levels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Autumn"))
bikes$Holiday <- factor(bikes$Holiday)

# The ten predictors, in this order, for every model in the lab.
# Not predictors: the date, the dew point temperature, Functioning_Day,
# and the count itself. The count defines High, so using it to predict
# High would be using the answer.
predictors <- c("Hour", "Temperature_C", "Humidity", "Wind_speed_m_s",
                "Visibility_10m", "Solar_Radiation_MJ_m2", "Rainfall_mm",
                "Snowfall_cm", "Seasons", "Holiday")
bikes <- data.frame(count = bikes$Rented_Bike_Count, High = bikes$High,
                    bikes[, predictors], date = bikes$Date)
str(bikes)
table(bikes$High)
summary(bikes$count)
length(unique(bikes$date))

# Question: How many open hours are there, and how many of them are
# High?
#
# Interpret: Hour is a number from 0 to 23 here. With two splits, a
# tree can still pick out a range of hours, for example 7 to 9.
```

We use the hours in three groups, each for one job.

```
open hours
├── training hours (70%)
│   ├── analysis hours (80% of training)    estimate every model;
│   │                                       cross-validation and
│   │                                       out-of-bag error stay here
│   └── validation hours (20% of training)  compare the five models
│                                           for High, once each
└── test hours (30%)                        report the one model you
                                            chose, once
```

The slides in class already showed results on these same test hours,
so today's test report is not a first look at them. It is still the
only number from the test hours that you report.

```{r}
#| label: split
# Why stratify? strata = High keeps the share of High hours almost the
# same in each group. The seed is reset right before each split, so
# everyone gets the same hours in each group.
set.seed(467)
outer_split <- initial_split(bikes, prop = 0.70, strata = High)
train <- training(outer_split)
test <- testing(outer_split)

set.seed(467)
inner_split <- initial_split(train, prop = 0.80, strata = High)
analysis <- training(inner_split)
validation <- testing(inner_split)

groups <- list(analysis = analysis, validation = validation, test = test)
sapply(groups, nrow)
round(sapply(groups, function(d) mean(d$High == "High")), 4)

# The split draws hours, not days. Count the dates that appear in both
# the training hours and the test hours.
length(unique(test$date))
length(intersect(unique(train$date), unique(test$date)))

# Benchmark: predict High for every hour.
mean(analysis$High == "High")

# Question: Predicting High for every analysis hour is right for what
# share of them? Keep that number. It is the benchmark for accuracy.
#
# Discuss: Most test dates also appear in the training hours. If the
# city wants a prediction for next week, why could this split look
# better than that prediction will be?
```

# 2. Grow, read and prune a tree

A classification tree splits the hours again and again on one
predictor at a time. Each final group is a leaf. The leaf predicts the
share of its analysis hours that were High: that is the tree's
probability of High.

We first grow a large tree with no penalty for size (cp = 0). The
complexity parameter (CP) is how much a split must reduce the error to
be kept. rpart also runs ten-fold cross-validation (CV) inside the
analysis hours: it estimates the tree on nine tenths and checks the
error on the last tenth, ten times.

```{r}
#| label: tree-grow
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
tree_controls <- rpart.control(cp = 0, maxdepth = 30, minsplit = 20,
                               minbucket = 7, xval = 10)
set.seed(467)
tree_full <- rpart(High ~ ., data = analysis[, c("High", predictors)],
                   method = "class", control = tree_controls)

n_splits <- function(fit) sum(fit$frame$var != "<leaf>")
n_splits(tree_full)

# Only the shape, without labels.
plot(tree_full, uniform = TRUE, compress = TRUE, margin = 0.01,
     main = paste("Full tree on the analysis hours:", n_splits(tree_full), "splits"))

# Question: How many splits does the full tree have? Could a planner
# use it as a list of rules?
```

```{r}
#| label: cp-table
cp_table <- tree_full$cptable
round(cp_table, 5)

# Interpret: Each line of the table is one subtree of the full tree.
# nsplit: its number of splits. rel error: its error on the analysis
# hours. xerror: its cross-validated error. xstd: the standard error of
# xerror. Both errors are relative to the root, the tree with no split,
# which predicts High for every hour.
#
# Question: As nsplit grows, rel error keeps falling. Does xerror keep
# falling too?
```

Two ways to choose a subtree from the table. The **minimum-CV** tree
has the lowest xerror. The **one-standard-error (one-SE)** tree is the
smallest subtree whose xerror is within one standard error of that
minimum. Both are computed from the table, as in class.

```{r}
#| label: prune
low <- which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"])
threshold_1se <- cp_table[low, "xerror"] + cp_table[low, "xstd"]
pick <- min(which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= threshold_1se))

# prune() keeps the splits whose CP is above the value we give it.
# Multiplying by a number just above 1 guards against rounding, so we
# get exactly the subtree on that line of the table.
tree_min <- prune(tree_full, cp = cp_table[low, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))
tree_1se <- prune(tree_full, cp = cp_table[pick, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))

cp_table[c(low, pick), ]
c(full = n_splits(tree_full), min_cv = n_splits(tree_min),
  one_se = n_splits(tree_1se))

# xerror is relative to the root. Times the root error, it is a share
# of analysis hours predicted wrong.
root_error <- mean(analysis$High == "Low")
round(c(min_cv = cp_table[low, "xerror"], one_se = cp_table[pick, "xerror"]) *
        root_error, 4)

# Question: How many splits do the two pruned trees have? How far apart
# are their cross-validated error rates, in percentage points?
```

```{r}
#| label: cv-error-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
leaves <- cp_table[, "nsplit"] + 1
cv_error <- cp_table[, "xerror"]
cv_se <- cp_table[, "xstd"]
# The subtrees with 1 and 2 leaves have much larger errors (see the
# table). They sit above the top of this plot.
plot(leaves, cv_error, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#156082",
     ylim = c(min(cv_error - cv_se), 0.35),
     xlab = "Leaves in the subtree (log scale)",
     ylab = "Cross-validated error, relative to the root",
     main = "Ten-fold cross-validated error of each subtree")
arrows(leaves, cv_error - cv_se, leaves, cv_error + cv_se,
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.02, col = "grey50")
abline(h = threshold_1se, lty = 2, col = "#C41230")
points(leaves[c(low, pick)], cv_error[c(low, pick)], pch = 1, cex = 2.2,
       col = "#C41230", lwd = 2)

# Interpret: The dashed line is the minimum xerror plus one standard
# error. The circles are the minimum-CV subtree and the one-SE subtree.
#
# Question: To the right of the one-SE tree, how much does the error
# fall as the tree grows? Is that fall larger than the bars?
```

```{r}
#| label: tree-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
#| column: page
# Each box: the predicted class, the probability of High, and the
# percent of analysis hours that reach that box. Left is yes.
rpart.plot(tree_1se, extra = 106, roundint = FALSE, faclen = 0,
           main = paste("One-SE tree:", n_splits(tree_1se), "splits"))

# Question: What is the first split? Which predictors appear in the
# first two levels of the tree?
```

Now follow two real hours down the tree. Both are 8 am hours from the
analysis hours, one in summer and one in winter.

```{r}
#| label: tree-path
eight_am <- analysis[analysis$Hour == 8, ]
two_hours <- rbind(eight_am[eight_am$Seasons == "Summer", ][1, ],
                   eight_am[eight_am$Seasons == "Winter", ][1, ])
two_hours[, c("date", "count", "High", "Temperature_C", "Humidity",
              "Rainfall_mm", "Seasons")]

# The probability of High from the tree, and the leaf (nn) each hour
# reaches.
leaf <- rpart.predict(tree_1se, two_hours, nn = TRUE)
leaf
# The conditions on the way to each leaf.
path.rpart(tree_1se, nodes = leaf$nn)

# Question: Write the summer hour's path as one rule a planner could
# read: "If ..., the probability of High is ...".
#
# Question: Was the winter hour High? Does the tree predict that it
# was? What does the tree not know about that hour?
```

The CP table measures error: the share of hours on the wrong side of
the 0.50 threshold. In section 7 we also compare models by the area
under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, the AUC, as in
Lab 5. The AUC uses the probabilities: it is the probability that a
random High hour gets a higher probability of High than a random Low
hour.

```{r}
#| label: tree-probabilities
# Every hour in a leaf gets the same probability. Count the different
# probabilities each tree gives to the analysis hours.
c(min_cv = length(unique(predict(tree_min, type = "prob")[, "High"])),
  one_se = length(unique(predict(tree_1se, type = "prob")[, "High"])))

# Question: Which tree can put the hours in a finer order from most to
# least likely High? Before section 7, which tree do you expect to have
# the higher AUC, and which the higher accuracy?
```

# 3. Compare bagging with a random forest

One tree changes a lot when the hours change a little. Bagging grows
many trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the analysis hours, and
averages their probabilities. A random forest does the same, and at
each split it also lets the tree choose only among a random subset of
the predictors. `mtry` is the size of that subset: 10 means all ten
predictors (bagging), and 3 means three of them, drawn again at every
split (the forest).

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap
# Why? A bootstrap sample draws as many hours as the analysis data has,
# with replacement. Some hours are drawn more than once and some are
# not drawn at all.
set.seed(467)
boot <- sample(nrow(analysis), replace = TRUE)
mean(!(seq_len(nrow(analysis)) %in% boot))

# Question: What share of the analysis hours did this one bootstrap
# sample leave out?
#
# Interpret: For each tree, the hours its bootstrap sample left out are
# its out-of-bag (OOB) hours. Each analysis hour is out of bag for
# about that share of the 500 trees. Averaging only those trees gives
# that hour an OOB prediction: a prediction from trees that never saw it.
```

```{r}
#| label: forests
# probability = TRUE: each forest predicts a probability of High.
# num.threads = 1 and seed = 467 make a second run on your own
# computer match the first. A neighbour on another operating system
# can differ in the third decimal. Compare your bagging with your
# forest, not with a neighbour.
bag <- ranger(High ~ ., data = analysis[, c("High", predictors)],
              num.trees = 500, mtry = 10, probability = TRUE,
              seed = 467, num.threads = 1)
forest <- ranger(High ~ ., data = analysis[, c("High", predictors)],
                 num.trees = 500, mtry = 3, probability = TRUE,
                 importance = "permutation", seed = 467, num.threads = 1)

# The OOB probability of Low and of High for the first analysis hours.
head(round(forest$predictions, 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: oob-error
# OOB classification error: the share of analysis hours whose OOB
# probability of High is on the wrong side of 0.50.
actual_high <- analysis$High == "High"
oob_error_bag <- mean((bag$predictions[, "High"] >= 0.5) != actual_high)
oob_error_forest <- mean((forest$predictions[, "High"] >= 0.5) != actual_high)
round(c(bagging = oob_error_bag, forest = oob_error_forest), 4)

# ranger also reports prediction.error. For a probability forest it is
# NOT the share of hours predicted wrong. It is the Brier score: the
# average squared difference between the probability of High and the
# outcome (1 for High, 0 for Low). Lower is better.
round(c(bagging = bag$prediction.error, forest = forest$prediction.error), 4)

# Question: Which model has the lower OOB error? By how many
# percentage points?
#
# Question: These OOB numbers use only the analysis hours. Why are they
# still an honest check, like cross-validation?
#
# Discuss: Bagging can use the strongest predictor at every split. Why
# could letting each split see only three predictors give a better
# average of trees?
```

# 4. Read variable importance

Permutation importance asks: if we shuffle one predictor across the
OOB hours, so that it no longer matches its hour, how much worse do the
OOB probabilities get? Here "worse" is the increase in the OOB Brier
score.

```{r}
#| label: importance-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8
importance <- sort(forest$variable.importance)
par(mar = c(4.5, 12, 2.5, 1))
barplot(importance, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = "#156082", border = NA,
        xlim = c(0, 1.05 * max(importance)),
        xlab = "Increase in OOB Brier score after shuffling the predictor",
        main = "Permutation importance, random forest (mtry = 3)")
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))
round(sort(forest$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE), 4)

# Interpret: Each bar is the increase in the OOB Brier score when that
# predictor is shuffled across the OOB hours.
#
# Question: Which three predictors matter most to the forest? Which
# matter least?
#
# Discuss: Temperature and Seasons carry some of the same information.
# How could that change the importance of each one?
#
# Question: Does the plot say whether warmer hours are more or less
# likely to be High? Where in this notebook would you look to find
# out?
```

# 5. Estimate boosting and compare learning rates

Boosting grows small trees one after another. Each new tree corrects
the current predictions a little. The learning rate is how much of each
new tree is added. The number of rounds is how many trees. The depth is
how many splits deep each tree may go; here it is 3 for both rates.

We choose the number of rounds by five-fold cross-validation inside the
analysis hours, using log-loss. Log-loss is the average of
$-\log(p)$, where $p$ is the probability the model gave to what
actually happened. A confident wrong probability costs a lot. Lower is
better.

The slide compared these two rates on the rental count, with root
mean squared error. Here both rates predict High, and the score is
log-loss.

```{r}
#| label: boost-cv
x_analysis <- analysis[, predictors]
d_analysis <- xgb.DMatrix(x_analysis, label = as.numeric(analysis$High == "High"))

# The same seed before each run gives both rates the same five folds.
set.seed(467)
cv_slow <- xgb.cv(params = list(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
                                learning_rate = 0.05, max_depth = 3, nthread = 1),
                  data = d_analysis, nrounds = 1000, nfold = 5, verbose = 0)
set.seed(467)
cv_fast <- xgb.cv(params = list(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
                                learning_rate = 0.5, max_depth = 3, nthread = 1),
                  data = d_analysis, nrounds = 1000, nfold = 5, verbose = 0)

# One line per round. test_logloss_mean is the average over the five
# held-out folds of the ANALYSIS hours. It is not our test hours.
head(cv_slow$evaluation_log, 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: boost-curves
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8
slow <- cv_slow$evaluation_log
fast <- cv_fast$evaluation_log
# The first rounds start above the top of the plot.
plot(slow$iter, slow$test_logloss_mean, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#156082",
     ylim = c(0, 0.5), xlab = "Boosting rounds (trees)",
     ylab = "Log-loss", main = "Five-fold cross-validated log-loss, depth 3")
lines(fast$iter, fast$test_logloss_mean, lwd = 2, col = "#C41230")
lines(slow$iter, slow$train_logloss_mean, lwd = 1, lty = 2, col = "#156082")
lines(fast$iter, fast$train_logloss_mean, lwd = 1, lty = 2, col = "#C41230")
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = c(2, 2, 1, 1), lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
       col = c("#156082", "#C41230", "#156082", "#C41230"),
       legend = c("rate 0.05, held-out folds", "rate 0.5, held-out folds",
                  "rate 0.05, training folds", "rate 0.5, training folds"))

# Interpret: Solid lines are the held-out folds. Dashed lines are the
# folds each model was estimated on.
#
# Question: Which rate reaches its lowest held-out log-loss in fewer
# rounds? What happens to the red solid line after that?
```

```{r}
#| label: boost-table
boost_table <- data.frame(
  rate = c(0.05, 0.5),
  best_round = c(which.min(slow$test_logloss_mean), which.min(fast$test_logloss_mean)),
  min_cv_logloss = c(min(slow$test_logloss_mean), min(fast$test_logloss_mean)),
  cv_logloss_1000 = c(slow$test_logloss_mean[1000], fast$test_logloss_mean[1000]),
  train_logloss_1000 = c(slow$train_logloss_mean[1000], fast$train_logloss_mean[1000])
)
boost_table

# Question: Compare the two minimum log-losses. Then compare the two
# log-losses after 1,000 rounds. Which comparison shows the difference
# between the rates?
#
# Discuss: Look at train_logloss_1000 for rate 0.5. What does that
# number say about the probabilities on the training folds, and what
# does the held-out line say?
```

```{r}
#| label: boost-fit
# The rate with the lower minimum CV log-loss, and its best round.
boost_rate <- boost_table$rate[which.min(boost_table$min_cv_logloss)]
boost_rounds <- boost_table$best_round[which.min(boost_table$min_cv_logloss)]
c(rate = boost_rate, rounds = boost_rounds)

# y is the factor High. xgboost predicts the probability of its second
# level, High.
set.seed(467)
boost <- xgboost(x = x_analysis, y = analysis$High, nrounds = boost_rounds,
                 learning_rate = boost_rate, max_depth = 3, nthreads = 1)

# Question: How many trees does the boosted model have? Why not stop at
# 1,000, or at the round where the training log-loss is lowest?
```

# 6. Predict the rental count

The same three ideas also predict the number of bikes rented. The
code is supplied and runs in a few seconds. The outcome is `count`, the
predictors are the same ten, and the hours are the same analysis hours.
We read one number for each model: the root mean squared error (RMSE)
on the validation hours, in rentals. The benchmark predicts the
average count of the analysis hours for every hour.

```{r}
#| label: count-models
count_data <- analysis[, c("count", predictors)]

# Regression tree, pruned with the one-SE rule, as in section 2.
set.seed(467)
count_full <- rpart(count ~ ., data = count_data, method = "anova",
                    control = tree_controls)
count_cp <- count_full$cptable
count_low <- which.min(count_cp[, "xerror"])
count_pick <- min(which(count_cp[, "xerror"] <=
                          count_cp[count_low, "xerror"] + count_cp[count_low, "xstd"]))
count_tree <- prune(count_full, cp = count_cp[count_pick, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))

# Regression forest, 500 trees, mtry = 3.
count_forest <- ranger(count ~ ., data = count_data, num.trees = 500, mtry = 3,
                       seed = 467, num.threads = 1)

# Boosting, rate 0.05, depth 3, rounds chosen by five-fold CV RMSE.
d_count <- xgb.DMatrix(x_analysis, label = analysis$count)
set.seed(467)
count_cv <- xgb.cv(params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eval_metric = "rmse",
                                 learning_rate = 0.05, max_depth = 3, nthread = 1),
                   data = d_count, nrounds = 1000, nfold = 5, verbose = 0)
count_rounds <- which.min(count_cv$evaluation_log$test_rmse_mean)
set.seed(467)
count_boost <- xgboost(x = x_analysis, y = analysis$count, nrounds = count_rounds,
                       learning_rate = 0.05, max_depth = 3, nthreads = 1)

c(tree_splits = n_splits(count_tree), boosting_rounds = count_rounds)
```

# 7. Compare class models and commit

Five models for High, all estimated on the analysis hours. Now each one
predicts the same validation hours. AUC uses the probabilities.
Accuracy uses a fixed threshold of 0.50: predict High when the
probability of High is at least 0.50. The 0.50 is fixed for everyone
so the models can be compared. It is not a claim about the best
threshold for the city.

```{r}
#| label: validation-compare
p_validation <- list(
  tree_min = predict(tree_min, validation, type = "prob")[, "High"],
  tree_1se = predict(tree_1se, validation, type = "prob")[, "High"],
  bagging = predict(bag, validation, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "High"],
  forest = predict(forest, validation, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "High"],
  boosting = predict(boost, validation[, predictors])
)
# TP: High hours predicted High. FP: Low hours predicted High.
# FN: High hours predicted Low. TN: Low hours predicted Low.
four_counts <- function(actual, p) {
  predicted_high <- p >= 0.5
  actual_high <- actual == "High"
  c(TP = sum(predicted_high & actual_high), FP = sum(predicted_high & !actual_high),
    FN = sum(!predicted_high & actual_high), TN = sum(!predicted_high & !actual_high))
}
validation_results <- data.frame(
  model = names(p_validation),
  AUC = sapply(p_validation, function(p)
    roc_auc_vec(validation$High, p, event_level = "second")),
  accuracy = sapply(p_validation, function(p)
    mean((p >= 0.5) == (validation$High == "High"))),
  t(sapply(p_validation, function(p) four_counts(validation$High, p))),
  row.names = NULL
)
transform(validation_results, AUC = round(AUC, 5), accuracy = round(accuracy, 4))

# Question: Rank the five models by AUC, then by accuracy. Is it the
# same order? Compare the two trees with what you expected in
# section 2.
#
# Question: How large is the AUC gap between the best tree and the
# best combined model? Between the top two models?
#
# Discuss: Would a difference in the fourth or fifth decimal of the
# AUC still be there with a different validation split? See
# after-class question 4.
```

**Before you commit.** Talk with the person next to you. The planners
want to know which hours will be High, and they want to be able to
follow the prediction. A tree can be printed as rules. The three
combined models cannot. Decide which model you would give them, using
only the validation table and what you know about each model. Then
write it down. Do not open the test hours to make this choice.

```{r}
#| label: commit
# Starting point only, so the chunk runs: the model with the highest
# validation AUC. Replace it with your choice, in quotes. The options
# are "tree_min", "tree_1se", "bagging", "forest" and "boosting".
my_model <- validation_results$model[which.max(validation_results$AUC)]
my_reason <- "Replace this sentence with your reason, in one sentence."

# The settings that stay locked for each model when it is estimated
# again on all the training hours.
locked <- data.frame(
  model = c("tree_min", "tree_1se", "bagging", "forest", "boosting"),
  settings = c(paste("classification tree, CP =", signif(cp_table[low, "CP"], 6)),
               paste("classification tree, CP =", signif(cp_table[pick, "CP"], 6)),
               "500 trees, mtry = 10, seed 467",
               "500 trees, mtry = 3, seed 467",
               paste("learning rate", boost_rate, "depth 3,", boost_rounds, "rounds"))
)
stopifnot(my_model %in% locked$model)
locked[locked$model == my_model, ]
my_reason

# Discuss: Choosing the highest validation AUC is one rule, not the
# only one. What are you giving up with the model you chose, and what
# are you getting?
```

# 8. Report the chosen model on test hours

The choice is made. Now estimate only that model again on all
`r nrow(train)` training hours (analysis and validation together),
with its locked settings, and predict the test hours once. On the
board: your model, its test AUC, accuracy, and the four counts, and
your one sentence.

```{r}
#| label: report-test
# Do not change my_model after reading these test results.
train_data <- train[, c("High", predictors)]
if (my_model %in% c("tree_min", "tree_1se")) {
  locked_cp <- if (my_model == "tree_min") cp_table[low, "CP"] else cp_table[pick, "CP"]
  final_full <- rpart(High ~ ., data = train_data, method = "class",
                      control = rpart.control(cp = 0, maxdepth = 30, minsplit = 20,
                                              minbucket = 7, xval = 0))
  final_model <- prune(final_full, cp = locked_cp * (1 + 1e-9))
  p_test <- predict(final_model, test, type = "prob")[, "High"]
} else if (my_model %in% c("bagging", "forest")) {
  final_model <- ranger(High ~ ., data = train_data, num.trees = 500,
                        mtry = if (my_model == "bagging") 10 else 3,
                        probability = TRUE, seed = 467, num.threads = 1)
  p_test <- predict(final_model, test, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "High"]
} else {
  set.seed(467)
  final_model <- xgboost(x = train[, predictors], y = train$High,
                         nrounds = boost_rounds, learning_rate = boost_rate,
                         max_depth = 3, nthreads = 1)
  p_test <- predict(final_model, test[, predictors])
}

test_auc <- roc_auc_vec(test$High, p_test, event_level = "second")
test_accuracy <- mean((p_test >= 0.5) == (test$High == "High"))
my_model
round(c(test_AUC = test_auc, test_accuracy = test_accuracy,
        always_High = mean(test$High == "High")), 4)

# Predictions run down the left side; actual hours run across the top.
test_confusion <- table(
  predicted = factor(ifelse(p_test >= 0.5, "High", "Low"), levels = c("Low", "High")),
  actual = test$High
)
test_confusion
sum(test_confusion)

# Question: How many test hours did your model predict High that were
# Low? How many High hours did it miss?
#
# Question: How much does your model add over predicting High for
# every test hour?
#
# Discuss: Name one thing this test report does not tell the city.
# Think about the dates in the test hours, where the weather inputs
# would come from for tomorrow, and the stations.
#
# Business implication: This is one report for one model chosen before
# the test hours were used. Estimating other models on the test hours
# now and keeping the best one would make this number a second choice,
# not a test.
```

# 9. After class: extra questions

Work these on your own after the hour. They use only the analysis and
validation hours. Do not change the model you reported on the board,
and do not use the test hours.

1. **More values of mtry.** The forest used 3 predictors per split and
   bagging used 10. Estimate the forest for every mtry from 1 to 10 and
   compare the OOB error and the OOB Brier score. Do the two measures
   choose the same mtry? Is the difference between 3 and the best value
   large?

2. **Learning rate and depth.** Repeat the cross-validation for depths
   1, 3 and 6, at learning rates 0.05 and 0.1. Which setting has the
   lowest minimum log-loss, and at how many rounds? Does a deeper tree
   need more rounds or fewer?

3. **A fuller count recommendation.** Use each count model's predicted
   count as a score for High: predict High when the predicted count is
   at least 500, the same definition as the outcome. Compare the AUC and
   accuracy on the validation hours with the class models in section 7.
   How many validation hours get a negative predicted count? Write two
   sentences for the planners: which count model would you use, and
   would you use it to flag High hours?

4. **Other splits.** Make five other analysis and validation splits of
   the same training hours (seeds 1 to 5). For each one, repeat the
   one-SE tree, bagging, the forest and boosting with the settings from
   class, and compare their validation AUCs. Is the same model highest
   every time? What does that say about the gap you saw in section 7?

5. **Importance in bagging.** Compute permutation importance for
   bagging and compare it with the forest. Then look at the average
   temperature by season. Why could Seasons matter differently when
   every split can use Temperature_C?

```{r}
#| label: after-class-stability
#| eval: false
# After class, change eval to true. Do not run these in the 75 minutes.
stability <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  sp <- initial_split(train, prop = 0.80, strata = High)
  a <- training(sp)
  v <- testing(sp)
  set.seed(467)
  ft <- rpart(High ~ ., data = a[, c("High", predictors)], method = "class",
              control = tree_controls)
  ct <- ft$cptable
  lo <- which.min(ct[, "xerror"])
  pk <- min(which(ct[, "xerror"] <= ct[lo, "xerror"] + ct[lo, "xstd"]))
  t1 <- prune(ft, cp = ct[pk, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))
  fb <- ranger(High ~ ., data = a[, c("High", predictors)], num.trees = 500, mtry = 10,
               probability = TRUE, seed = 467, num.threads = 1)
  ff <- ranger(High ~ ., data = a[, c("High", predictors)], num.trees = 500, mtry = 3,
               probability = TRUE, seed = 467, num.threads = 1)
  set.seed(467)
  fx <- xgboost(x = a[, predictors], y = a$High, nrounds = boost_rounds,
                learning_rate = boost_rate, max_depth = 3, nthreads = 1)
  auc_v <- function(p) roc_auc_vec(v$High, p, event_level = "second")
  data.frame(seed = s,
             tree_1se = auc_v(predict(t1, v, type = "prob")[, "High"]),
             bagging = auc_v(predict(fb, v, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "High"]),
             forest = auc_v(predict(ff, v, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "High"]),
             boosting = auc_v(predict(fx, v[, predictors])))
}))
round(stability, 4)
```
